channel.title: The Lost Generation
channel.description: Posts in the discussion thread "The Lost Generation" - “For my whole life, I didn’t know if I even really existed. But I do, and people are starting to notice.”

item.title: Re: The Lost Generation
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

Article proceeds normally with several recovery logs detailing the circumstances surrounding particular subjects, most of which were only discovered after perpetrating acts of violence or suicide.

When you say 'subjects' here, do you mean 'the SCP' or 'people affected by the SCP'?

My broader concerns with this are two fold. Firstly, it kinda feels like this is really blurring the lines between 'real' and 'not real' to a point where I don't really have a clear idea of how this works. Specifically, you mention people have a like 'uncanny valley' reaction to them that leads them to be ostracised; but you also have this thing where folk who meet them can end up assuming they've been friends for a long time and it kinda feels like there's this awkward mesh where they both can and can't infiltrate society?

Thematically, a lot of this reminds me of SCP-4857 except it feels a lot blunter in it's questions.

My other big concern is that I'm not actually sure what this article will look like: the hook section indicates that there's meant to be this whole thing about being unsure if there's like, innocent people who have been arrested for crimes (and…I'm really not sure how that works: the implication of the infohazard is it only adds fake memories surrounding the SCP, not fake memories in general, and in turn, how can someone falsely remember murdering someone if they're still alive cos that implies they aren't an instance of the SCP?); but the additional notes imply this is meant to be much more about the effects of isolation in themes and I'm not sure how you're intending blending the two together.

item.title: Re: Forum Criticism Team - Junior Staff Post
item.content:encoded: Thanks for the critique, there's a 400 word limit so I couldn't go into a ton of detail. Essentially they're identical to normal humans and they can, on paper, interact with the world around them just like we do but they're limited by the fact that regular people can kind of tell that there's something "off" about them and avoid them instinctively. Their nonexistence is both literal and metaphorical; they have no past and their inability to form connections with others ensures they have no future either.

item.title: Re: Forum Criticism Team - Junior Staff Post
item.content:encoded: I’m sorry, I’m new here. I find the concept of an actual lost people interesting, but I don’t think I really understand how they… exist or don’t exist, I guess? I can understand that they appear, but I don’t understand how they interact with the world around them. What makes them not real. It seems to me more like they pop into existence. It reminded me of 1504 because of the way they almost aren’t real- no one can perceive what he’s really saying or doing. I actually think they should make it more similar to him, as an example of how to make a person “not real.” Again, sorry, just got here.

Krystal_Cipher, per the Site's Criticism Policy found here: http://www.scp-wiki.net/criticism-policy

Forum critique should be relatively in-depth.

Try to make sure you give enough criticism that an author can tell the quality of their entire concept/draft. What exactly about this concept do you find interesting? What parts do you not understand? It might be easier for the author to clear things up if they knew. Could you elaborate? Adding on, what elements of this concept remind you of SCP-1504? What can the author do to avoid making the concept too similar to SCP-1504?

item.title: The Lost Generation
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Drama/Emotional

Elevator Pitch:

  • A race of human that technically doesn't exist. Instances appear spontaneously in unobserved areas, such as empty rooms or abandoned buildings, at approximate ages from early teens to late middle age.
  • For all intents and purposes, they are identical to baseline humans and have false memories of past events (primarily negative), providing the illusion of personal history. Images or descriptions of these subjects have a targeted infohazardous effect, in that people who appear in these "memories" have no knowledge of the subject until introduced or "reminded" of their physical characteristics, upon which they suddenly recall having known them for extended periods of time. Digital databases rewrite themselves to resolve discrepancies.
  • When interacting with or recalling instances, baseline humans tend to subconsciously experience a mild "uncanny valley" effect, causing them to feel a sense of revulsion they can't quite put into words. The resulting ostracism often leads to mood and personality disorders.

Central Narrative: Article proceeds normally with several recovery logs detailing the circumstances surrounding particular subjects, most of which were only discovered after perpetrating acts of violence or suicide.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: In the Special Containment Procedures section it's briefly mentioned that tests utilizing D-Class personnel at a specific site are to be put on hold until further notice, with referral to an incident log. The log in question details the discovery of a D-Class who was supposedly imprisoned for first degree murder of someone who was still alive, calling into question how many innocent people the Foundation has thrown at Keters and such.

Additional Notes: Humans are social creatures. People who live isolated lives, either because of mental issues that adversely affect their ability to form relationships or bad circumstances, are at great risk for adverse psychological effects. Normally humanoid SCPs like 1788 or 2852 have some quality that make them easily identifiable, but I thought "What about ones where you usually can't tell until it's too late?"
